mcq.question: Which values can `std::uniform_int_distribution<int> die(1, 6)` produce?

options.A: 1 to 5, because the upper bound is excluded
options.D: Any int, scaled into the range by the caller

mcq.explanation: Unlike iterator ranges, `uniform_int_distribution` uses a closed interval [a, b]. `uniform_real_distribution` is the one that uses a half-open interval [a, b).

mcq.question: Why do the tests create engines with `make_engine(42)` instead of seeding from `std::random_device`?

options.B: A fixed seed makes every run produce the same sequence, so failures can be reproduced
options.C: A fixed seed produces better-quality random numbers

mcq.explanation: Reproducibility is what makes randomised code testable and debuggable. Real sessions can still use `random_device` for an unpredictable seed.

bonus.question: Different standard libraries may implement `std::normal_distribution` differently, so the same seed can give different numbers on Windows and Linux. When does that matter, and how would you guarantee identical results everywhere?
Write a failing test for an `advantage(spec, engine)` function that rolls twice and keeps the higher total, then implement it and check its average is higher than a single roll.
